title: Caching
summary: Keeping copies of data where they are fast to read: hit ratio, where caches live, and why a small cache often does most of the work.

blocks.p: Most of the time an app spends on a request goes to fetching data: a database query, a call to another service, a file from disk. Many of those fetches return the same answer as the last time someone asked.
Fetching it again costs time and load. A database that answers the same query 1,000 times a second does 1,000 times the work it needs to.

A **cache** keeps copies of recent answers in a place that is faster to read than the original, usually memory. Before fetching, the app checks the cache. If the answer is there, that is a **hit**. If not, it is a **miss**: the app fetches from the database and keeps a copy for next time.
The share of reads that are hits is the **hit ratio**. It decides how much work the cache saves. At a 90% hit ratio, the database sees one read in ten.

blocks.caption: An app reading 50 different keys through a cache with room for 20. The cache starts empty. Watch the hit ratio climb as popular keys fill it.

blocks.h3: Why a small cache does a lot

blocks.p: Requests are rarely spread evenly. A few items, such as the front page or a popular product, get most of the reads. A cache with room for those few items catches most requests, even though it holds a small part of the data.
When reads are spread evenly over every item, the same cache helps far less. Its hit ratio is about its size divided by the number of items.

list: **In the browser.** The HTTP caching rules in the CDN lesson let the browser reuse responses without asking at all.
**At the edge.** A CDN keeps copies near users.
**In the app's memory.** The fastest option, but each server has its own copy, and copies on different servers can disagree.
**In a shared cache service.** A separate in-memory store, such as Redis or Memcached, that every app server reads. One copy, one network round trip away.
**In the database.** Databases keep recently read pages in memory too. Reads that hit that memory skip the disk.

**Facebook built a large shared cache.** Its paper [Scaling Memcache at Facebook](https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi13/technical-sessions/presentation/nishtala) describes memcached as a demand-filled look-aside cache in front of its databases. The app checks the cache first and fills it after a miss.
**Cache what is read often and changes rarely.** Product pages and user profiles cache well. A bank balance that must always be current does not.
**A cache is a copy.** It can be out of date, and it can be lost. The data must still live somewhere authoritative. The invalidation lesson covers keeping copies fresh.
**Plan for an empty cache.** After a restart, every read is a miss. If the database can't handle the full load, a cache restart becomes an outage.

blocks.p: Change the cache size, and whether a few keys are popular or every key is equally likely. Watch the hit ratio and the database reads.

blocks.caption: 50 keys behind a cache. Compare 20 slots with popular keys against 20 slots with even reads.

list: A cache keeps copies of answers somewhere faster than the original.
The hit ratio decides how much load the cache removes.
Uneven popularity lets a small cache catch most reads.
A cache is a copy: it can be stale, and it can be empty after a restart.
